title: The elephant's chain
hookLine: a restless elephant, a chain, and the helps Ramana allows
carry: a name of God steadies the reaching mind

lines: A TRUNK THAT GRABS AT EVERYTHING.
GIVE IT A CHAIN TO HOLD.
cards: An elephant walking down a street swings its trunk from side to side. It grabs at a banana stall, a branch, the edge of someone's cart. Nothing malicious.
A trunk just reaches. Now give that elephant a chain to hold in its trunk. It carries the chain, and the reaching stops.
Ramana Maharshi uses that picture in Who Am I?, in the middle of a plain, practical answer about how to steady a mind that won't settle.

teach.h: THE MAIN ROAD: WHO AM I?
teach.b: The question who am I? is the main road in the text. But when Ramana is asked about other practices, he doesn't wave them away. He gives each one a place.

teach.h: BREATH AND MIND SHARE ONE SOURCE.
teach.b: The mind and the breath, he says, come from the same source, so when the breath is controlled, the mind quiets too. But the quiet lasts only as long as the breath is held still.
When the breath moves again, the mind goes back to its wandering. Breath control is a help, not the destination.

teach.h: JAPA: A NAME OF GOD STEADIES THE MIND.
teach.b: Then japa, repeating a name of God, or resting the attention on a form of God. Here's where the elephant comes in.
The mind, like that trunk, keeps reaching for one thing after another. Give it one thing to hold, a name, a form, and it steadies. A mind held on one thing, Ramana says, finds the inquiry easier.
This is one of the most widely kept Hindu practices. Many Hindus carry a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads, and say a name on each one: Ram, Krishna, Om Namah Shivaya.

So Ramana isn't telling anyone their practice is wrong. The grandmother with her beads, the person who watches the breath, the person who asks who am I: each gets a place, with a plain note on what each one does.

how: Some who follow Ramana combine self-inquiry with chanting a divine name, meditating on a form of God, or watching the breath, using these to steady the mind before or alongside asking 'who am I?'.

o: a teacher who banned every practice but one question
the sage who made room for the breath and God's name
a king's minister who wrote rules for the royal court

games.q: the helps along the way — tap the pairs.
p: one thing to hold: a name or form
a string of 108 beads for japa

s: Ramana says the mind and the breath come from the same source
that's why controlling the breath quiets the mind, for a while.
in Who Am I?, he dismisses chanting and meditation on God as useless
he gives them a place: they steady the mind so the inquiry comes more easily.
he says breath control alone ends the mind's wandering for good
he warns the quiet lasts only while the breath is held; then the mind wanders again.

games.q: an elephant's trunk keeps grabbing at stalls and carts as it walks. what steadies it, in Ramana's picture?
o: tie the trunk down so it can't move.
give it a chain to hold.
lead it down an empty street.
games.why: given one thing to hold, the trunk stops reaching. a name or form of God does the same for the mind, Ramana says, and a steady mind finds the inquiry easier.

practice: First give the trunk a chain: the breath going in and out at the nose, or, if you pray, a name of God from your own practice, repeated quietly, bringing the attention back each time it reaches for something else.
When the mind feels a little steadier, let the chain go and ask once, softly: who am I? Rest wherever that question leaves you.

wordCard.voice: Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of who am I?, who also made room for the breath and japa, the name of God, as ways to steady a reaching mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prana, the breath and life-force. Ramana says breath and mind share one source.

carryVoice: Your line: a name of God steadies the reaching mind. Tomorrow, the last of these four days: where Ramana says happiness lives. See you there.
